The bridge closed on a Tuesday, which everyone agreed was inconsiderate.

On Monday, a thing could still be planned around. By Wednesday, people had begun inventing alternatives. But Tuesday caught the town halfway through its intentions, with groceries on the wrong bank and a dentist who could see his waiting room from his kitchen window but had to drive forty minutes to reach it.

The sign said NINE DAYS.

Underneath, in smaller letters, it said THANK YOU FOR YOUR PATIENCE, as though patience were something already handed over.

Mara owned a boat.

It was a flat-bottomed aluminum boat, purchased years earlier during a period when she believed she might become the sort of person who fished. She had bought a hat, too. The hat had been more successful.

At seven on Wednesday morning, she dragged the boat down the bank and rowed across for bread.

On the other side, Mr. Voss was standing with a briefcase.

“Are you going back?”

“I live over there.”

“Yes,” he said. “Of course.”

He looked at the boat with the expression of someone considering a very large dog.

“You can get in,” Mara said.

He did, holding his briefcase above his knees.

Halfway across, he asked what she charged.

“Nothing.”

“That isn’t sustainable.”

“Neither is standing on the bank.”

By noon, she had carried eleven people, a folding bicycle, and a cake that required its own crossing because the woman holding it refused to sit anywhere except the middle.

“It’s a retirement cake,” she explained.

“Does that make it heavier?”

“It makes it irreplaceable.”

Mara accepted this.

On Thursday, someone left a wooden box beside her landing place. FERRY, it said in black paint. Beneath that: PAY WHAT’S FAIR.

The box contained six coins, a grocery token, and a note that said, *Fair to whom?*

She recognized Mr. Voss’s handwriting from the notices he posted about parking.

She put the note in her coat pocket.

***

The river was not impressive. It had none of the grandeur that persuaded people to describe water as ancient. It was thirty yards wide, brown after rain, and usually occupied by ducks with modest ambitions.

Still, in the middle of it, the town changed.

The bakery sign became unreadable. The traffic lights could be seen but not obeyed. People who spent their days being useful had to sit with their hands in their laps.

Some disliked this.

A man in a silver watch asked whether Mara could row faster.

“Yes,” she said.

After a moment, he understood that this was the entire answer.

Others took to the crossing immediately.

Two schoolgirls began meeting at the boat each afternoon although one of them lived on the side where they started. An elderly woman brought a flask and poured tea into the lid. A mechanic who always smelled of warm rubber closed his eyes for the whole journey.

Mara had driven buses for thirty-one years. She knew what tired people looked like when they finally trusted someone else to deliver them.

She did not speak to the mechanic.

***

On the ninth day, the sign changed.

The new sign said ESSENTIAL ADDITIONAL WORKS.

“That sounds expensive,” Mara told the man fastening it to the barrier.

“It’s not my wording.”

“Nothing ever is.”

He tightened the last bolt and asked whether she could take him across. His van was on the other side.

By then, the landings had acquired improvements.

Someone cut steps into the steeper bank. Someone else installed a rail. The bakery sent yesterday’s rolls in a paper sack each morning, which caused fierce discussion about whether a roll became less yesterday’s when eaten outdoors.

Mr. Voss drew up a timetable.

Mara refused it.

He revised it into “approximate operating expectations.”

She allowed him to pin it to a tree.

The boat worked badly in hard rain and not at all after dark. It carried fewer people than needed carrying. Twice Mara woke with such stiff shoulders that she stayed in bed while the town rediscovered the road.

Nobody mistook it for an efficient arrangement.

Even so, when the bridge reopened after five weeks, people seemed oddly reluctant to celebrate.

***

There was a ribbon.

The mayor thanked the engineers, the contractors, the residents, and, after someone prompted him, “our temporary maritime service.”

Mara stood at the back in her fishing hat.

Mr. Voss presented her with the contents of the wooden box, counted and entered on a sheet of paper.

“You’ve deducted nothing for costs,” he said.

“I didn’t keep receipts.”

He looked pained, but handed it over.

Afterward, she walked down to the landing. Without footsteps coming through the grass, she could hear the little knocks the boat made against its stake.

She was untying the rope when the mechanic appeared above her.

“Finished?” he asked.

“Bridge is open.”

“I saw.”

He came down the steps but stopped short of getting in.

“I’m not in a hurry,” he said.

Mara looked at him, then shifted the paper sack of rolls from the passenger seat.

The mechanic stepped aboard. She pushed them away from the bank and settled the oars.

For a while he watched the bridge. Then, as he usually did, he closed his eyes.

Mara took the longer crossing, a little downstream, where the current was gentler. There was nobody waiting on either bank, and she wanted to save her shoulders for the row back.
